questions.stem:
A 36-year-old man has had 3 weeks of gradually worsening dry cough, low-grade fever, and shortness of breath on exertion. He has never been tested for HIV. Temperature is 38.1 C (100.6 F), respiratory rate 24/min, and oxygen saturation 93% on room air at rest, falling to 84% after walking a few meters. Lung examination is nearly normal. Chest x-ray shows diffuse bilateral reticular interstitial infiltrates. Serum lactate dehydrogenase and 1,3-beta-D-glucan are elevated. HIV testing is positive, and the CD4 count is 60/mm3.

Which of the following is the preferred test to confirm the diagnosis?
choices: Bronchoalveolar lavage with methenamine silver staining
Sputum culture on standard bacterial media
Mycobacterial blood culture held for up to 8 weeks of growth

explain.html:
Opportunistic infections are stratified by CD4 count, and below 200 the most common one in AIDS is Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP), a ubiquitous inhaled fungus that often appears before the patient knows he has HIV. The organism provokes an intense alveolar inflammatory reaction that fills the air spaces with frothy, honeycombed material and impairs oxygen exchange. Clinically this produces a subacute illness over weeks with fever, nonproductive cough and dyspnea, a nearly normal lung exam, and the hallmark precipitous drop in oxygenation with exertion. The chest x-ray shows diffuse bilateral reticular or interstitial infiltrates, and LDH and 1,3-beta-D-glucan are often elevated, but neither is specific.

Because Pneumocystis does not grow in routine culture, the diagnosis rests on seeing the organism: the preferred specimen is bronchoalveolar lavage, with induced sputum less invasive but less sensitive. Gomori methenamine silver stains the cyst walls, and Wright-Giemsa shows cysts and trophozoites, while PCR cannot distinguish infection from colonization. Here the desaturation from 93% to 84% after a few steps, the interstitial pattern and a CD4 of 60 make lavage with silver stain the confirming test.
explain.table:
Opportunistic infectionKey confirming test
Pneumocystis pneumoniaBronchoalveolar lavage with methenamine silver stain
Cryptococcal meningitisOpening pressure and cryptococcal antigen on lumbar puncture
Disseminated histoplasmosisHistoplasma antigen in urine or serum
Disseminated MACMycobacterial blood culture (up to 8 weeks)
CMV retinitisDilated funduscopic exam
why: Pneumocystis does not grow on routine culture media, so a bacterial sputum culture cannot confirm it.
Cryptococcal antigen evaluates cryptococcal disease, which presents mainly as subacute meningoencephalitis, not exertional hypoxia with interstitial infiltrates.
Urine antigen is the sensitive rapid test for disseminated histoplasmosis, not Pneumocystis.
Mycobacterial blood culture diagnoses disseminated MAC, which causes fever, sweats, diarrhea and cytopenias rather than a primarily pulmonary picture.
explain.takeaway: In HIV with CD4 below 200, subacute dry cough, exertional desaturation and bilateral interstitial infiltrates indicate PCP, confirmed by bronchoalveolar lavage with methenamine silver stain because Pneumocystis cannot be cultured.

explain.objective: Describe the presentation, diagnosis, and treatment of the major opportunistic infections in HIV.

questions.stem:
A 33-year-old man with untreated HIV infection has 3 weeks of slowly worsening headache, fever, and malaise. His family reports he has become forgetful and lethargic. He has no neck stiffness or photophobia. CD4 count is 28/mm3. CT of the head shows no mass lesion. Lumbar puncture results:

[[labs 0]]

Which of the following is the preferred initial (induction) treatment?
choices: Liposomal amphotericin B followed by itraconazole
Amphotericin B plus flucytosine for 2 weeks

explain.html:
Cryptococcus neoformans is an oval, encapsulated, yeast-like fungus found in soil and bird droppings that enters by inhalation and has a tropism for the central nervous system. Risk begins at a CD4 below 100 and disease usually appears below 50 as a subacute meningoencephalitis: gradually worsening headache, fever, malaise and encephalitic features such as lethargy and memory loss, often without neck stiffness or photophobia. On lumbar puncture the hallmark is elevated intracranial pressure, the cryptococcal antigen is highly specific when positive, and the cell count may be low because of a poor inflammatory response, which is a negative prognostic sign.

Treatment runs in three phases. Induction is amphotericin B plus flucytosine for 2 weeks, with close monitoring of creatinine and electrolytes and generous hydration, followed by consolidation with fluconazole 400 to 800 mg daily for 8 weeks and then maintenance fluconazole 200 mg daily; repeat lumbar puncture manages the high pressure. This man's opening pressure of 38 with only 8 white cells and a high-titer capsular antigen at a CD4 of 28 is cryptococcal meningitis, so he needs the amphotericin plus flucytosine induction.
explain.table:
PhaseRegimenDuration
InductionAmphotericin B plus flucytosine2 weeks
ConsolidationFluconazole 400 to 800 mg daily8 weeks
MaintenanceFluconazole 200 mg dailyUntil on ART with CD4 above 100, undetectable viral load, azole over 1 year
why: Fluconazole 200 mg daily is the maintenance phase and is too weak to start therapy for active meningitis.
Liposomal amphotericin followed by itraconazole is the regimen for disseminated histoplasmosis, not cryptococcal meningitis.
Pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine and leucovorin treat cerebral toxoplasmosis, which causes ring-enhancing mass lesions that this CT excluded.
High-dose TMP-SMX treats Pneumocystis pneumonia and has no role in cryptococcal meningitis.
explain.takeaway: Cryptococcal meningitis in HIV (CD4 usually below 50, high opening pressure, positive cryptococcal antigen, few cells) is induced with amphotericin B plus flucytosine for 2 weeks, then consolidated and maintained with fluconazole.

explain.objective: Describe the presentation, diagnosis, and treatment of the major opportunistic infections in HIV.

questions.stem:
A 45-year-old woman with advanced HIV infection (CD4 count 40/mm3) is brought to the emergency department with 1 week of headache, confusion, and a new seizure. She is febrile. The admitting team is concerned about an opportunistic infection of the central nervous system and wants to sample the cerebrospinal fluid.

Which of the following should be done before the lumbar puncture, and why?
choices: Serum cryptococcal antigen, because a positive result makes the lumbar puncture unnecessary
Head CT, because a mass lesion could cause herniation when pressure is released
Blood cultures, because bacteremia is a contraindication to lumbar puncture
Toxoplasma IgG, because a negative result rules out all brain lesions
Electroencephalogram, because seizure activity raises intracranial pressure

explain.html:
Several opportunistic infections and tumors in advanced HIV produce mass lesions in the brain: toxoplasmosis with multiple ring-enhancing lesions, and similar lesions from CNS lymphoma, tuberculosis and cryptococcosis. A mass lesion raises intracranial pressure. A lumbar puncture removes fluid from below and changes the pressure gradient, and in the setting of mass effect that pressure change can precipitate brain herniation. For this reason the lecture's rule is that in HIV a CT scan of the head is done before any lumbar puncture.

This woman has a CD4 of 40, headache, confusion, fever and a new seizure, which raises the possibility of a focal lesion such as toxoplasmosis or lymphoma as much as meningitis. Imaging first tells the team whether the lumbar puncture is safe; the cerebrospinal fluid can then be sent for PCR, cell count and cryptococcal antigen if it is.
why: A serum antigen cannot exclude a mass lesion and does not make the lumbar puncture safe or unnecessary.
Bacteremia is not the safety concern before a lumbar puncture here; the risk is herniation from a mass lesion.
A negative Toxoplasma IgG does not exclude lymphoma, tuberculosis or cryptococcal mass lesions.
An electroencephalogram does not detect a mass lesion and is not the step that protects against herniation.
explain.takeaway: In HIV with neurologic symptoms, a head CT precedes lumbar puncture because opportunistic mass lesions raise intracranial pressure and removing fluid can precipitate herniation.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Describe the presentation, diagnosis, and treatment of the major opportunistic infections in HIV.

questions.stem:
A 39-year-old man with HIV who stopped his antiretroviral therapy a year ago has 10 days of headache, personality change, and new weakness of his right arm. He owns two cats and often eats rare steak. CD4 count is 62/mm3. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain shows three ring-enhancing lesions in the basal ganglia and at the gray-white junction, with surrounding edema. Serum IgG against an intracellular protozoan is positive.

Which of the following is the preferred treatment?

explain.html:
Toxoplasma gondii is acquired from cats and undercooked or raw meat, and in HIV disease it presents as reactivation of prior infection with a predilection for the central nervous system, at CD4 counts below 100. Symptoms depend on where the lesions sit: headache, altered mental status, seizures, personality change and focal deficits. Contrast CT or MRI usually shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions, and a positive IgG supports the diagnosis because it marks the prior infection that is reactivating. Ring enhancement is not specific, so CNS lymphoma, tuberculosis and cryptococcosis remain on the differential.

The preferred treatment is pyrimethamine plus sulfadiazine plus leucovorin, with TMP-SMX also listed; alternatives include pyrimethamine plus clindamycin and atovaquone-based regimens. This man has cats, eats rare steak, has a CD4 of 62, three ring-enhancing lesions with right arm weakness and a positive IgG, which is cerebral toxoplasmosis.
explain.table:
FeatureCerebral toxoplasmosisPrimary CNS lymphoma
AgentToxoplasma gondii (reactivation)Epstein-Barr virus
ImagingUsually multiple ring-enhancing lesionsMass lesion
Supporting testPositive Toxoplasma IgGEBV PCR of CSF, brain biopsy
TreatmentPyrimethamine, sulfadiazine, leucovorinNot an antimicrobial regimen
why: Amphotericin B plus flucytosine is induction therapy for cryptococcal meningitis, not for a protozoan brain abscess.
Ganciclovir treats CMV, whose CNS disease is dementia, ventriculoencephalitis or radiculopathy rather than multiple ring lesions with positive Toxoplasma IgG.
Macrolide-based combinations with ethambutol treat Mycobacterium avium complex, a disseminated marrow and node infection.
Nitazoxanide with ART is tried for cryptosporidiosis, a diarrheal protozoan, not a CNS infection.
explain.takeaway: Cerebral toxoplasmosis in HIV is reactivation at CD4 below 100 with multiple ring-enhancing lesions and positive IgG, and is treated with pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine and leucovorin.

explain.objective: Describe the presentation, diagnosis, and treatment of the major opportunistic infections in HIV.

questions.stem:
A 51-year-old man with untreated HIV infection reports 2 weeks of floaters and a growing blind spot in his left eye, without pain or redness. CD4 count is 18/mm3. Dilated funduscopic examination shows fluffy yellow-white retinal lesions mixed with areas of intraretinal hemorrhage along the vessels.

Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

explain.html:
Cytomegalovirus is a double-stranded DNA virus, and most people with active disease in AIDS are seropositive, so illness reflects reactivation of prior infection at CD4 counts below 50. CMV causes a wide spectrum of disease: retinitis, esophagitis, colitis and central nervous system infection. CMV retinitis is a sight-threatening, full-thickness necrotizing retinitis in one or both eyes, diagnosed by dilated funduscopic exam. The classic fundus shows fluffy yellow-white retinal lesions with intraretinal hemorrhages, the tomato and cheese pizza appearance.

Treatment for CMV disease is intravenous ganciclovir or oral valganciclovir. This man has painless floaters and an enlarging blind spot at a CD4 of 18 with exactly that fundus, so oral valganciclovir is the appropriate treatment among the choices.
why: Fluconazole is an antifungal for Candida and Cryptococcus and does not treat a viral retinitis.
Acyclovir is not the drug listed for CMV; ganciclovir and valganciclovir are.
Itraconazole follows amphotericin B for disseminated histoplasmosis and has no activity against CMV.
TMP-SMX treats Pneumocystis and toxoplasmosis, not CMV.
explain.takeaway: CMV retinitis is reactivation at CD4 below 50 with fluffy yellow-white necrotizing lesions and intraretinal hemorrhages, treated with IV ganciclovir or oral valganciclovir.

explain.objective: Describe the presentation, diagnosis, and treatment of the major opportunistic infections in HIV.

questions.stem:
A 46-year-old man with untreated HIV infection has 6 weeks of fevers, drenching night sweats, a 7-kg weight loss, and watery diarrhea. Examination shows hepatosplenomegaly and enlarged lymph nodes. Chest x-ray is clear. CD4 count is 14/mm3.

[[labs 0]]

A mycobacterial blood culture grows acid-fast bacilli after several weeks.

Which drug class is the most active and reliable component of treatment?

explain.html:
Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) is ubiquitous, acquired by inhalation or ingestion, usually as primary infection, and causes disease at CD4 counts below 50. It presents as a disseminated infection rather than one confined to an organ, with an insidious onset over several weeks of fever, weight loss, night sweats and diarrhea. It predominantly affects bone marrow and lymph nodes, so patients may have lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, marked anemia, neutropenia and an elevated alkaline phosphatase. Diagnosis is by mycobacterial blood culture, which can take up to 8 weeks, or biopsy of an affected node or marrow.

Treatment is a two- to three-drug combination guided by susceptibility testing, and the most active and most reliable agents are the macrolides, clarithromycin and azithromycin. Rifabutin, ethambutol, quinolones and injectable aminoglycosides are partner drugs. This man's sweats, diarrhea, hepatosplenomegaly, hemoglobin of 7.8, neutropenia and alkaline phosphatase of 410 at a CD4 of 14 with acid-fast bacilli in a mycobacterial blood culture are disseminated MAC.
why: Quinolones are listed partner agents, not the most active or reliable component.
Injectable aminoglycosides such as amikacin are add-on agents, not the core of therapy.
Echinocandins are antifungals used as alternatives for Candida and have no antimycobacterial activity.
Nucleoside analog antivirals such as ganciclovir act on viruses and have no activity against mycobacteria.
explain.takeaway: Disseminated MAC at CD4 below 50 causes fever, sweats, weight loss, diarrhea, cytopenias and raised alkaline phosphatase, and is treated with a macrolide-based two- to three-drug combination.

explain.objective: Describe the presentation, diagnosis, and treatment of the major opportunistic infections in HIV.

questions.stem:
A 31-year-old woman with HIV infection (CD4 count 160/mm3) notices white patches in her mouth for a week. They are painless. Examination shows creamy white plaques on the buccal mucosa, tongue, and palate that are easily wiped off with a tongue depressor, leaving a red base. She swallows without difficulty or pain.

Which of the following is the most likely diagnostic finding and appropriate treatment?
choices: Encapsulated yeast on India ink; amphotericin
Yeast on a potassium hydroxide prep; fluconazole

explain.html:
Candida, usually C. albicans, is normal flora of the oropharynx, and immunosuppression allows overgrowth that in HIV causes oropharyngeal or esophageal infection. Oropharyngeal candidiasis presents as painless, creamy white plaques on the buccal mucosa, tongue and palate that can be easily removed with a tongue depressor. Diagnosis is mostly by direct visualization, and scraping the patches shows yeast on a KOH prep. Esophageal disease causes odynophagia and retrosternal pain, may occur without visible thrush and is confirmed by endoscopy.

The preferred treatment is fluconazole; oral disease can also be treated topically with clotrimazole troches or nystatin suspension, and echinocandins and amphotericin are alternatives. This woman's painless wipeable plaques with a red base and normal swallowing at a CD4 of 160 are oral thrush, so the expected finding is yeast on KOH and the treatment is fluconazole.
why: Inclusion-bearing large cells and ganciclovir describe CMV, which causes painful ulcers, not wipeable white plaques.
Acid-fast oocysts are found in stool in protozoal diarrhea, and TMP-SMX treats Cystoisospora, not thrush.
India ink shows the capsule of Cryptococcus, a meningitis agent treated with amphotericin, not oral thrush.
Multinucleated giant cells and acyclovir fit a herpes simplex lesion, which forms painful ulcers rather than painless wipeable plaques.
explain.takeaway: Oral candidiasis presents as painless creamy white plaques that scrape off, KOH prep shows yeast, and fluconazole is the preferred treatment.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Describe the presentation, diagnosis, and treatment of the major opportunistic infections in HIV.

questions.stem:
A 40-year-old man who grew up in the Ohio River valley and recently moved to New Jersey has HIV infection that has been untreated for years (CD4 count 95/mm3). He has 4 weeks of fever, fatigue, night sweats, weight loss, and a dry cough. Examination shows lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly. Chest x-ray shows diffuse small nodular opacities.

Which of the following is the most sensitive rapid test for his likely diagnosis?
choices: Serum coccidioidal IgM and IgG serology
Lavage fluid with silver stain for cysts
Urine and serum antigen for the dimorphic fungus

explain.html:
The endemic mycoses act as opportunistic infections in people who live in or travel to endemic areas. Histoplasmosis is linked to the US Midwest, Puerto Rico and Central or South America, usually appears when the CD4 is below 150, and in HIV is often disseminated. It presents with constitutional symptoms (fever, weight loss, fatigue, night sweats), pulmonary symptoms, and enlarged lymph nodes, liver and spleen. Coccidioidomycosis, by contrast, is tied to the desert southwest with risk rising below a CD4 of 250.

The rapid diagnostic test for disseminated histoplasmosis is Histoplasma antigen in urine or serum, which is highly sensitive and specific, while cultures of marrow, node or lavage can take several weeks. Treatment is liposomal amphotericin B for more than 2 weeks, then oral itraconazole. This man grew up in the Ohio River valley and has fever, sweats, cough, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly and nodular opacities at a CD4 of 95, so the urine and serum antigen is the test to send.
explain.table:
FeatureHistoplasmosisCoccidioidomycosis
Endemic areaUS Midwest, Puerto Rico, Central and South AmericaUS desert southwest, Central and South America
CD4 riskUsually below 150Below 250
DiagnosisUrine or serum antigen; culture takes weeksCulture, histopathology, serology (IgM, IgG)
TreatmentLiposomal amphotericin B, then itraconazoleAmphotericin B then azole; meningitis high-dose fluconazole
why: Cryptococcal antigen evaluates cryptococcal disease, which presents mainly as meningoencephalitis rather than hepatosplenomegaly with nodular lungs.
Coccidioidal serology fits desert southwest exposure, not an upbringing in the Ohio River valley.
Silver-stained cysts in lavage diagnose Pneumocystis, which does not cause lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly.
Mycobacterial blood culture diagnoses MAC, takes up to 8 weeks and is not a rapid test.
explain.takeaway: Disseminated histoplasmosis (Midwest or Puerto Rico exposure, CD4 below 150) is diagnosed rapidly by urine or serum Histoplasma antigen and treated with liposomal amphotericin B followed by itraconazole.

questions.stem:
A 37-year-old man with HIV infection and a CD4 count of 140/mm3 needs prophylaxis against Pneumocystis pneumonia. He had a severe rash with mucosal blistering the last time he took a sulfonamide antibiotic, so trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole cannot be used. His physician chooses an oral alternative but first orders a blood test.

Which drug and pretreatment test are most appropriate?
choices: Atovaquone; HLA-B*5701 genotype before the first dose

explain.html:
When the CD4 count is between 100 and 200, primary prophylaxis covers Pneumocystis. TMP-SMX is preferred, daily or three times weekly. When it cannot be used, the alternatives listed are atovaquone, dapsone and monthly aerosolized pentamidine. Dapsone is an oral option, and the lecture flags it with a specific precaution: check G6PD first. Dapsone is an oxidant drug, so a patient with G6PD deficiency is at risk of hemolysis.

This man has a CD4 of 140 and a severe blistering reaction to a sulfonamide, which rules out TMP-SMX. His physician chooses an oral alternative and orders a blood test first, which matches dapsone with a G6PD level. Azithromycin and fluconazole do not prevent Pneumocystis, and pentamidine for prophylaxis is aerosolized rather than oral.
explain.table:
PCP prophylaxis optionRoute and note
TMP-SMXOral, preferred; daily or three times weekly
AtovaquoneOral alternative
DapsoneOral alternative; check G6PD first
PentamidineAerosolized, monthly
why: Atovaquone is an acceptable alternative, but HLA-B*5701 testing goes with abacavir, not atovaquone.
Pentamidine prophylaxis is given monthly by aerosol, not orally, and kidney function is not the flagged precaution.
Azithromycin is MAC prophylaxis and does not prevent Pneumocystis.
Fluconazole is an antifungal for Candida and Cryptococcus and does not prevent Pneumocystis; neither fungus gets primary prophylaxis.
explain.takeaway: When TMP-SMX cannot be used for Pneumocystis prophylaxis, alternatives are atovaquone, dapsone (check G6PD first because of hemolysis risk) or monthly aerosolized pentamidine.

explain.objective: Describe primary and secondary prophylaxis for opportunistic infections in HIV.

questions.stem:
A 44-year-old man started antiretroviral therapy 8 months ago when his CD4 count was 90/mm3, together with daily trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis. He has never had an opportunistic infection. His recent results are below. He asks whether he can stop the prophylaxis.

[[labs 0]]

Which of the following is the most appropriate advice?
choices: Continue until the CD4 count exceeds 500/mm3
Stop ART and continue prophylaxis instead

explain.html:
Prophylaxis in HIV depends on immune reconstitution with antiretroviral therapy. Primary prophylaxis can be discontinued when the patient is on effective ART and the CD4 count has stayed above the relevant threshold for more than 3 months. There is a second route for Pneumocystis: with a CD4 between 100 and 200, PCP prophylaxis can stop if the patient is on ART with an undetectable viral load for more than 12 months. Secondary prophylaxis, given after an adequately treated infection, follows the same logic and generally stops once the CD4 is above threshold for at least 3 months, and for most infections 6 months.

This man started ART at a CD4 of 90 with TMP-SMX and has never had an opportunistic infection, so his prophylaxis is primary. His CD4 has been above 200 on two measurements 4 months apart with an undetectable viral load, which satisfies the 3-month rule, so prophylaxis can stop now while ART continues.
why: Prophylaxis is not lifelong once immune reconstitution on ART is sustained.
The stopping threshold for Pneumocystis and toxoplasmosis coverage is 200, not 500.
ART is what restores immunity, so stopping it would undo the reason prophylaxis can end.
No prophylaxis is needed now, so switching to another agent indefinitely is unnecessary.
explain.takeaway: Primary opportunistic infection prophylaxis can stop when the CD4 count stays above its threshold for more than 3 months on effective ART.

explain.objective: Describe primary and secondary prophylaxis for opportunistic infections in HIV.

questions.stem:
A 35-year-old man with untreated HIV infection (CD4 count 110/mm3) notices several painless purple, irregular plaques on his legs and the roof of his mouth that have grown over 2 months. They do not blanch with pressure.

Which virus is most closely associated with these lesions?

explain.html:
Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also called Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus, causes Kaposi sarcoma, a vascular malignancy. Its skin lesions are violaceous, irregular plaques, mucosa such as the palate can be involved, and visceral involvement can occur. Treatment is ART, with chemotherapy as needed. It is one of three opportunistic agents of malignancy in HIV, alongside EBV with primary CNS lymphoma and HPV with cervical and anal cancer.

This man has painless purple irregular plaques on his legs and palate growing over 2 months at a CD4 of 110, and they do not blanch, which fits a vascular tumor rather than an infection or rash. The virus most closely associated is HHV-8.
explain.table:
VirusMalignancy or disease in HIV
HHV-8Kaposi sarcoma
Epstein-Barr virusPrimary CNS lymphoma
HPV 16 and 18Cervical and anal cancer
CMVRetinitis, esophagitis, colitis
JC virusProgressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy
why: Epstein-Barr virus drives primary CNS lymphoma in HIV, not violaceous skin plaques.
HPV 16 is linked to cervical and anal cancer, not vascular skin tumors.
CMV causes retinitis, esophagitis and colitis, not a vascular tumor.
JC virus causes progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, a brain disease, not skin plaques.
explain.takeaway: Kaposi sarcoma, violaceous vascular plaques of skin and mucosa with possible visceral spread, is caused by HHV-8 and treated with ART plus chemotherapy as needed.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Describe the opportunistic infections that act as agents of malignancy in HIV.

questions.stem:
A 42-year-old woman with untreated HIV infection (CD4 count 45/mm3) has 2 weeks of nonproductive cough and progressive dyspnea. Oxygen saturation is 86% on room air, and arterial blood gas shows a markedly reduced partial pressure of oxygen. Chest x-ray shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates. Bronchoalveolar lavage shows foamy, honeycombed alveolar material, and cysts are seen with a methenamine silver stain. She has no drug allergies.

In addition to the first-line antimicrobial, which drug should be started because of her degree of hypoxia?

explain.html:
Pneumocystis jirovecii is a fungus, yet the preferred therapy is an antibacterial: high-dose trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX), 15 to 20 mg/kg per day of the trimethoprim component in divided doses. The damage in PCP is not only from the organism; it provokes an intense inflammatory reaction in the alveoli, producing an interstitial pneumonitis and alveoli filled with frothy honeycombed material. That inflammation is what impairs gas exchange. When oxygenation is significantly impaired, a corticosteroid such as prednisone is added to decrease lung inflammation. Other treatment options for the organism itself are atovaquone, intravenous pentamidine, dapsone plus trimethoprim, and primaquine plus clindamycin.

This patient has silver-staining cysts in foamy alveolar material, an oxygen saturation of 86% and a markedly reduced arterial oxygen, so her degree of hypoxia is the decisive finding that calls for prednisone alongside TMP-SMX. Azoles, flucytosine, antivirals and macrolides belong to other opportunistic infections and add nothing here.
explain.table:
DrugRole in this lecture
High-dose TMP-SMXPreferred PCP treatment
PrednisoneAdded to PCP therapy when oxygenation is significantly impaired
FluconazoleCandidiasis; cryptococcal consolidation and maintenance
FlucytosineWith amphotericin B for cryptococcal induction
GanciclovirCMV disease
AzithromycinMAC treatment and prophylaxis
why: Fluconazole treats Candida and cryptococcal disease and has no role against Pneumocystis or its inflammation.
Flucytosine is paired with amphotericin B for cryptococcal induction and does not treat PCP.
Ganciclovir treats cytomegalovirus, which causes retinitis, esophagitis and colitis rather than silver-staining alveolar cysts.
Azithromycin is used against Mycobacterium avium complex and does not reduce alveolar inflammation in PCP.
explain.takeaway: PCP, a fungal infection, is treated with high-dose TMP-SMX, and a corticosteroid is added when hypoxia is significant to blunt the alveolar inflammation that impairs gas exchange.

questions.stem:
A 44-year-old woman with advanced HIV infection (CD4 count 30/mm3) has 4 weeks of progressive confusion, lethargy, weight loss, and night sweats, and she had a seizure yesterday. MRI shows a single large enhancing periventricular mass. Toxoplasma IgG is negative. Lumbar puncture is judged safe, and cerebrospinal fluid is sent for nucleic acid testing.

The virus most likely to be detected in her cerebrospinal fluid primarily infects which cell type?

explain.html:
Three opportunistic infections in HIV act as agents of malignancy: Epstein-Barr virus with primary CNS lymphoma, HHV-8 with Kaposi sarcoma, and HPV with cervical and anal cancer. Epstein-Barr virus is a DNA herpesvirus that infects B cells, and in HIV its oncogenic potential increases, producing primary central nervous system lymphoma. The lymphoma presents with CNS symptoms such as lethargy, confusion and seizures together with constitutional symptoms. Diagnosis combines imaging, EBV PCR of the cerebrospinal fluid when a lumbar puncture is safe, and brain biopsy.

This woman has a single enhancing periventricular mass, confusion, a seizure, weight loss and night sweats at a CD4 of 30, and her negative Toxoplasma IgG makes reactivated toxoplasmosis unlikely. The virus her cerebrospinal fluid will show is EBV, and it infects B lymphocytes, the cells from which the lymphoma arises.
explain.table:
VirusMalignancy in HIV
Epstein-Barr virus (infects B cells)Primary CNS lymphoma
HHV-8 (KSHV)Kaposi sarcoma, a vascular malignancy
HPV 16 and 18Cervical cancer; anal cancer
why: CD4 T cells are the target of HIV itself, not of the herpesvirus that drives this lymphoma.
Oligodendrocytes are the target in progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy from JC virus, which is not a single enhancing mass with constitutional symptoms.
A vascular tumor points to HHV-8 and Kaposi sarcoma, which presents as violaceous skin and mucosal plaques, not a brain mass.
Retinal involvement is the hallmark of CMV retinitis, not a periventricular brain mass.
explain.takeaway: Primary CNS lymphoma in advanced HIV is driven by EBV, a B-cell-tropic DNA herpesvirus, and EBV PCR of the cerebrospinal fluid supports the diagnosis.

questions.stem:
A 38-year-old woman with advanced HIV infection (CD4 count 25/mm3) has 3 weeks of severe pain on swallowing and retrosternal pain. Oral examination shows no white plaques. She took fluconazole for a week without improvement. Upper endoscopy shows large, shallow ulcers in the distal esophagus without plaques. Biopsy shows enlarged cells containing both intranuclear and intracytoplasmic inclusions.

The drug most appropriate for this infection acts against a virus with which of the following genomes?

explain.html:
Odynophagia in advanced HIV has two main opportunistic causes in this lecture. Candida esophagitis causes odynophagia and retrosternal pain, may occur without visible thrush, shows plaques at endoscopy and responds to fluconazole. CMV esophagitis causes pain with swallowing at CD4 counts below 50 and is diagnosed by endoscopy with biopsy, where pathology shows large cells with intranuclear and intracytoplasmic inclusions. CMV colitis presents with bloody diarrhea, abdominal pain and fever and is diagnosed the same way.

This woman failed a week of fluconazole, has no thrush or esophageal plaques, and her biopsy shows inclusion-bearing enlarged cells, so the cause is cytomegalovirus. CMV is a double-stranded DNA virus, and the drug for it, ganciclovir or valganciclovir, acts against that virus.
explain.table:
FeatureCandida esophagitisCMV esophagitis
EndoscopyPlaquesUlcers without plaques
BiopsyYeast on path and cultureLarge cells with intranuclear and intracytoplasmic inclusions
TreatmentFluconazoleGanciclovir or valganciclovir
why: No virus with a positive-sense RNA genome is taught as a cause of inclusion-cell esophagitis in HIV.
Single-stranded RNA with reverse transcriptase describes a retrovirus such as HIV itself, not the cause of the ulcers.
Partially double-stranded circular DNA is not the genome of CMV, which is double-stranded DNA.
No negative-sense RNA virus is taught as a cause of this esophagitis.
explain.takeaway: CMV esophagitis presents with odynophagia and ulcers without plaques, biopsy shows large cells with intranuclear and intracytoplasmic inclusions, and the double-stranded DNA herpesvirus is treated with ganciclovir.

questions.stem:
A 34-year-old man recently returned from a trip abroad and has 5 weeks of profuse, watery, non-bloody diarrhea, crampy abdominal pain, low-grade fever, and a 6-kg weight loss. He has untreated HIV infection, with a CD4 count of 70/mm3. Stool examination with a modified acid-fast stain shows large oval oocysts about 25 micrometers long that stain red; no smaller 5-micrometer oocysts are seen.

Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment, in addition to starting antiretroviral therapy?

explain.html:
Three protozoan infections cause diarrheal opportunistic illness at CD4 below 100: cryptosporidiosis, microsporidiosis and cystoisosporiasis. All are acquired fecal-orally by ingesting oocysts or spores and all cause prolonged non-bloody diarrhea, abdominal symptoms, fever, malabsorption and wasting. They are separated on stool studies by size on the modified acid-fast stain, which stains oocysts red: Cryptosporidium is 5 to 7 micrometers, Cystoisospora is about 25 micrometers, and microsporidial spores are 1 to 2 micrometers.

All three resolve with immune reconstitution on antiretroviral therapy. Cystoisospora is treated with TMP-SMX, while Cryptosporidium has inconsistent results with nitazoxanide or paromomycin, which can be used but always together with ART. This man's large 25 micrometer red oocysts with no small ones identify Cystoisospora, so TMP-SMX is added to ART.
explain.table:
OrganismSize on stainTreatment besides ART
Cryptosporidium5 to 7 micrometer oocystsNitazoxanide or paromomycin, inconsistent
CystoisosporaAbout 25 micrometer oocystsTMP-SMX
Microsporidia1 to 2 micrometer sporesART for immune reconstitution
why: Nitazoxanide is tried for Cryptosporidium, whose oocysts are 5 to 7 micrometers, not 25.
Paromomycin is an inconsistent option for Cryptosporidium, not Cystoisospora.
Amphotericin B treats fungal infections such as cryptococcal meningitis and histoplasmosis, not protozoal diarrhea.
Fluconazole is an antifungal for Candida and Cryptococcus and has no role against a protozoan.
explain.takeaway: Among AIDS protozoal diarrheas (CD4 below 100), large 25 micrometer acid-fast oocysts identify Cystoisospora, treated with TMP-SMX, whereas small oocysts mean Cryptosporidium, which depends on ART.

questions.stem:
A 29-year-old woman is newly diagnosed with HIV infection. She has no symptoms. Antiretroviral therapy is started today. Baseline results:

[[labs 0]]

She has no drug allergies.

Which of the following is the most appropriate prophylaxis to start now?
choices: No prophylaxis until the CD4 count falls below 50/mm3

explain.html:
Primary prophylaxis prevents opportunistic infections before they happen and starts when the CD4 count is below 200. Coverage widens as the count falls. Between 100 and 200 the target is Pneumocystis, with TMP-SMX preferred. Between 50 and 100 the target is both toxoplasmosis and Pneumocystis, and the preferred agent is double-strength TMP-SMX daily because one drug covers both. Below 50, MAC no longer needs coverage if ART is being started; otherwise weekly azithromycin 1200 mg is used. There is no primary prophylaxis for cryptococcus, Candida, CMV or the diarrheal protozoa.

This woman has a CD4 of 78, a positive Toxoplasma IgG (and toxoplasmosis in HIV is reactivation of that latent infection), a normal G6PD and no allergies, and she starts ART today. Daily double-strength TMP-SMX is therefore the single right choice, and prophylaxis can later stop once her CD4 stays above threshold on ART for more than 3 months.
explain.table:
CD4 countCoverPreferred
100 to 200PneumocystisTMP-SMX daily
50 to 100Pneumocystis and toxoplasmosisTMP-SMX DS daily
Below 50MAC only if ART is not being startedWeekly azithromycin 1200 mg
AnyNo primary prophylaxis for cryptococcus, Candida, CMV, diarrheal protozoaNone
why: MAC coverage is unnecessary when ART is being started and her CD4 is above 50, and fluconazole is not given as primary prophylaxis.
Aerosolized pentamidine covers Pneumocystis only and leaves her Toxoplasma-seropositive brain unprotected.
Primary prophylaxis for CMV is not recommended.
Prophylaxis starts below 200, and her count of 78 is already well below that threshold.
explain.takeaway: At CD4 50 to 100, daily double-strength TMP-SMX is the preferred primary prophylaxis because it covers both Pneumocystis and toxoplasmosis, and MAC prophylaxis is unnecessary when ART is started.

explain.objective: Describe primary and secondary prophylaxis for opportunistic infections in HIV.
